extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, drama students, and critics interested in dramatic composition (especially tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama according to Aristotelian poetics: how tragedy arises, its defining features, constituent parts, and rules for plot, character, diction, song, spectacle, and magnitude. Useful for writers and analysts of dramatic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as poetic instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from the human instinct of imitation; men are the most imitative of animals, and learn earliest through imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imitation (representation of actions, characters, life) as the basis of poetic composition; recognize imitation is natural from childhood and central to pleasure in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in contemplating likenesses
rubrics_metrics.description: People take pleasure in the faithful reproduction of objects (even those that are painful in reality), because contemplating a likeness involves learning and recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft vivid, accurate representations and details (execution, colouring, etc.) to produce aesthetic pleasure even when subject matter is sad or ignoble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct for harmony and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides imitation, humans possess an instinct for harmony and rhythm; metres are sections of rhythm and aided the rise of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to rhythm and musical qualities (meter, harmony) as fundamental components of poetic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres originate from disposition and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry diverged into serious (noble) and trivial (mean) imitation according to writers’ aptitudes; different metres and forms suit different genres (e.g., iambic for lampooning, hexameter for epic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metre and form appropriate to the moral tone and aims of the piece; recognise historical affinities (iambics for comic/lampooning speech, hexameters for epic narration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not narrative; effecting through pity and fear the proper purgation (catharsis) of those emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the work meets all components: seriousness of action, completeness, adequate magnitude, suitable linguistic embellishment (meter/song), enacted rather than merely told, and aims at arousing and purging pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness, completeness, and magnitude (qualities of a tragic action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be serious (not trivial), complete (a whole with beginning, middle, end), and of a certain magnitude (large enough to be unified and graspable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an action that forms a whole (has causal sequence), is important in consequence, and is of a size that the audience can apprehend in memory and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language embellished: rhythm, harmony, song
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic language should be embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; different parts of the play may employ different kinds of artistic ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate metrical and musical elements appropriately—some parts may be purely verse, others include song—to enhance the imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of action (showing not telling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should be in the form of action (dramatized) rather than mere narrative or report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor enacted scenes and incidents over chains of narrated events; the plot must be presented through agents acting rather than through descriptive exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: effect through pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy effects the purgation (catharsis) of pity and fear by arousing and then resolving those emotions through the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents and reversals to evoke pity and fear in order to achieve the purgative emotional arc; the emotional effect is a primary aim of tragic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Diction (lexis), Thought (dianoia), Spectacle (opsis), and Song (melopoiia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or compose a tragedy by accounting for each part—plot and character as primaries, diction and thought as modes of expression, song as chief embellishment, spectacle as external and least artistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the arrangement of incidents) is the first principle and most important element of tragedy; the structure of incidents determines the quality of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize coherent causal sequencing (beginning–middle–end), meaningful reversals and recognitions, and an integrated whole when building or judging a play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure: beginning, middle, end; unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole plot has a beginning (that which does not follow from something else), a middle (follows and is followed), and an end (follows from something and has nothing following). Unity of plot is unity of action, not unity of hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure causal necessity or probability links parts so the plot neither begins nor ends at random; choose a single, coherent action to structure the work rather than compiling disparate adventures of one hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and limits of length
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of adequate magnitude—long enough to allow a change from good to bad fortune or vice versa, yet short enough to be apprehended as a whole (memory/perception limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set length so the sequence of events can be grasped by the audience; dramatic competitions/time limits are external constraints, but natural dramatic magnitude is determined by unity and comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and Recognition as chief plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) are the greatest elements of emotional interest in tragedy and are parts of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-crafted reversals and recognitions; these are powerful sources of pity and fear and crucial to a successful tragic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character secondary to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (ethos) holds the second place; actions determine happiness or misfortune, so character serves the action rather than being primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters insofar as they enable and reveal action; avoid relying on speeches or finely painted portraits alone—actions and incidents must drive the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as proof and general truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent, of proving or stating general truths in given circumstances; found where something is demonstrated or enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to articulate motives, to advance arguments, and to make statements appropriate to circumstances; thought supports plot through purposeful discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — expression and metrical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the interpretation through naming and applies both in verse and prose (including metrical arrangement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft precise wording and appropriate metrical arrangement; diction should reveal character and suit the medium (colloquial vs. elevated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melopoiia) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the embellishments, song holds the chief place—melody and musical elements greatly contribute to the tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat song/choral elements as central embellishments rather than mere ornament; use them strategically in parts of the play for emotional and structural effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) is least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has an emotional attraction but is the least artistic part of tragedy and is more dependent on stagecraft than on the poet's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on spectacular effects to carry artistic merit; prioritize plot, character, diction, thought, and song over visual machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions, not speeches, make tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere string of speeches expressive of character, however well finished in diction and thought, will not produce the essential tragic effect; action and constructed incidents are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid replacing plotted incidents with eloquent speeches; ensure the drama proceeds through enacted events that lead to emotional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity is unity of action (not of episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of the plot requires that all parts belong to the single action such that removing or moving a part alters the whole; irrelevant episodes are not parts of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every episode or incident contributes causally or probabilistically to the central action; trim extraneous adventures that do not affect the unified outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate meter for colloquial speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Iambic measure is the most colloquial of meters; conversational speech tends to fall into iambic lines more than into other meters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing dialogue or colloquial exchange, consider iambic rhythm as naturally suited to conversational tones; reserve hexameter and other meters for narrative/epic modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic composition evolves from improvisation to formal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy and comedy originated in improvisation and gradually developed elements (actors, chorus changes, scenography, measures) until they found a natural form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize historical/formal constraints and that refined dramatic forms (actor numbers, scene painting, meters) evolved to serve the art; adopt established dramatic conventions where they serve unity and effect.
